title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(e) Basic Research Payments
description: 26 U.S.C. § 41(e) gives eligible C corporations a 20% credit on payments to qualified universities and scientific organizations for basic research.
summary: This page explains Basic Research Payments under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e), the provision granting eligible C corporations a 20% research credit on cash paid under written agreements to qualified universities and scientific organizations for basic research. The credit applies to payments exceeding the Qualified Organization Base Period Amount, while non-incremental amounts flow into regular qualified research expenses at 65%.

body.text: This page explains Basic Research Payments under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e), the provision granting eligible C corporations a 20% research credit on cash paid under written agreements to qualified universities and scientific organizations for basic research. The credit applies to payments exceeding the Qualified Organization Base Period Amount, while non-incremental amounts flow into regular qualified research expenses at 65%.
Executive Overview and Statutory Architecture

Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(e), codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(e), establishes a targeted federal tax credit for cash payments made by eligible corporate taxpayers to qualified educational and scientific research institutions for the performance of basic research.

Since the initial enactment of the federal Research and Experimentation (R&E) Tax Credit under the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (Pub. L. 97-34) and its permanent extension under the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113), federal tax policy has addressed a structural economic divergence: private commercial enterprises systematically underinvest in foundational, theoretical science because its financial returns are long-term, technically uncertain, and difficult to appropriate exclusively through near-term proprietary commercialization. To remedy this market failure, Section 41 bifurcates the federal research tax credit into distinct statutory tracks. Standard Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—comprising internal employee wages, consumable supplies, computer rental or lease costs, and third-party contract research directed at commercial product or process development—are governed by 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(b), whereas corporate patronage of foundational academic and scientific inquiry is governed separately by 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(2) and § 41(e) (alongside a third track for energy research consortia under § 41(a)(3)).

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(2) and § 41(e)(1)(A), the federal tax code grants a non-refundable general business credit equal to 20% of a corporate taxpayer's Basic Research Payments that exceed a specialized historical baseline known as the Qualified Organization Base Period Amount (QOBPA). Unlike standard contract research expenses, where payments to external non-employee vendors are immediately subjected to a 65% statutory inclusion cap (a 35% reduction) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) (or 75% for payments to qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C)), incremental Basic Research Payments above the QOBPA threshold enter the 20% credit calculation at 100% of the qualifying cash expenditure. Furthermore, the portion of a corporation's current-year Basic Research Payments that does not exceed the QOBPA is not forfeited; instead, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(1)(B) directs that this non-incremental baseline amount flows into the taxpayer's general QRE pool as a standard contract research expense for purposes of 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), where it is subject to the 65% inclusion limitation under Section 41(b)(3)(A). Simultaneously, to prevent double counting, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(C) mandates that the incremental Basic Research Payments taken into account under Section 41(a)(2) shall neither be treated as general QREs under Section 41(a)(1)(A) nor be included in the computation of the regular base amount under Section 41(a)(1)(B).

The strategic complexity of Section 41(e) expands significantly when integrated with state-level research and development (R&D) tax credit regimes. Key innovation jurisdictions, most notably California under R&TC Section 23609 and Massachusetts under M.G.L. Chapter 63, Section 38M, incorporate the federal mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(e) by reference while substantially modifying credit rates, substantive research definitions, geographic nexus rules, federal conformity dates, and corporate group utilization caps.
Federal Statutory Mechanics of 26 U.S.C. Section 41(e)
Interaction Between the Section 41(d) Four-Part Test and Section 41(e)(7)(A)

To qualify for the research credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41, research activities must satisfy the baseline requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), commonly referred to as the Four-Part Test. First, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures must qualify as specified research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174 (or, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, following the enactment of Public Law 119-21, domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A), meaning they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product or process. Second, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the investigation must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying fundamentally on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)–(3), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (the Permitted Purpose test, relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality). Fourth, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that evaluates technical alternatives through modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error, or prototyping.

For Basic Research Payments, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(A) imposes a more restrictive substantive threshold. The statute defines "basic research" verbatim as "any original investigation for the advancement of scientific knowledge not having a specific commercial objective". In addition, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(A)(i) and (ii) expressly exclude from the definition of basic research any basic research conducted outside of the United States and any basic research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities.

This statutory architecture creates an inherent compliance tension for corporate tax departments. Under general QRE rules, expenditures must bear a nexus to a trade or business of the taxpayer; to bridge this gap for foundational academic grants, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(D) provides a dedicated statutory rule stating that, for purposes of applying Section 41(b)(1) to Section 41(e), any qualifying Basic Research Payments shall be treated as an amount paid in carrying on a trade or business of the taxpayer in the taxable year in which it is paid, without regard to the prepaid contract research timing limitation of Section 41(b)(3)(B). Nevertheless, to satisfy the substantive definition of Section 41(e)(7)(A), the university research agreement cannot target a specific commercial product design, near-term engineering deliverable, or immediate proprietary application. Consequently, audit-defensible basic research agreements must be framed around pre-competitive, foundational scientific inquiries within a scientific discipline relevant to the corporation's industry rather than applied engineering milestones for an existing commercial product line.
Eligible Corporate Taxpayers and Statutory Entity Exclusions

Access to the federal Basic Research Payment credit is strictly circumscribed by corporate tax classification. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A), Basic Research Payments can only be made by a "corporation". Furthermore, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(E) explicitly restricts the definition of an eligible "corporation" by excluding S corporations as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 1361 (under § 41(e)(7)(E)(i)), personal holding companies as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 542 (under § 41(e)(7)(E)(ii)), and service organizations as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 414(m)(3) (under § 41(e)(7)(E)(iii)).

Because sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability companies taxed as partnerships, S corporations, and other pass-through entities are statutorily barred from claiming the incremental credit under Section 41(e)(1)(A), rapidly scaling technology and biotechnology companies that elect pass-through status to avoid double taxation on corporate dividends cannot utilize the 20% basic research credit. Utilization of Section 41(e) is therefore structurally concentrated among established Subchapter C corporations that possess both the eligible corporate entity structure and the balance-sheet capitalization required to fund multi-year university endowments and institutional research grants.
Qualified Organizations and the Written Agreement Mandate

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A), a Basic Research Payment must be paid in cash during the taxable year—excluding non-cash property contributions or in-kind equipment transfers—pursuant to a contemporaneous written agreement between the corporate taxpayer and a "Qualified Organization" (QO). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(e)(2)(B), the basic research must be performed directly by the receiving Qualified Organization, except where the recipient is a qualifying scientific grant-making conduit organization described in Section 41(e)(6)(C) or Section 41(e)(6)(D).

In the actual text of the Internal Revenue Code, energy research consortia are governed separately by 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(3) (providing a flat 20% credit for energy research payments to an energy research consortium), 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D) (providing a 100% inclusion rate for energy research payments to eligible small businesses, universities, and federal laboratories), and 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(6) (defining an energy research consortium), rather than Section 41(e)(6). Instead, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(6)(A)–(D) defines four specific categories of Qualified Organizations eligible to receive Basic Research Payments:

cells: Any educational organization that is an institution of higher education within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 3304(f) and is described in 26 U.S.C. § 170(b)(1)(A)(ii) (maintaining a regular faculty and curriculum with a regularly enrolled body of students in physical attendance).
Must perform the basic research directly under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A)(ii).

Any organization not described in § 41(e)(6)(A) that is described in 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) and is exempt from tax under 26 U.S.C. § 501(a), is organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research, and is not a private foundation.
Must perform the basic research directly under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A)(ii).

Any organization described in 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) (other than a private foundation) or § 501(c)(6), exempt from tax under § 501(a), organized and operated primarily to promote scientific research by qualified educational institutions described in § 41(e)(6)(A) pursuant to written research agreements, and currently expending substantially all of its funds (or substantially all of the basic research payments received by it) for grants to, or contracts for basic research with, an educational institution described in § 41(e)(6)(A).
Exempt from direct performance under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(B); acts as a grant or contract conduit to higher education institutions.

Any organization not described in § 41(e)(6)(B) or (C) that is described in 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) and exempt under § 501(a) (other than a private foundation), is established and maintained by an organization established before July 10, 1981 meeting such requirements, is organized and operated exclusively for making grants to § 41(e)(6)(A) educational institutions pursuant to written research agreements for basic research, and elects (revocable only with the Secretary's consent) to be treated as a private foundation for Title 26 purposes other than the § 4940 investment income excise tax.
Exempt from direct performance under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(B); acts as a grant conduit to higher education institutions.

body.text: From an administrative enforcement perspective, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS)—as reflected in IRS Research Credit Audit Technique Guides (ATGs), including the Aerospace Industry Research Credit ATG and the general IRC § 41 Research Credit ATG—instructs examiners to scrutinize the written contracts governing external and university-sponsored research. Consistent with 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A)(i) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i), the written agreement must be entered into prior to the performance of the research and must clearly delineate that the payments fund foundational scientific investigation rather than routine product testing, quality control, or commercial software engineering.
Mathematical Mechanics of the Qualified Organization Base Period Amount (QOBPA)

Because the Section 41(e) credit is designed to incentivize incremental corporate funding of academic science above historical norms, the 20% federal rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(2) applies strictly to current-year Basic Research Payments that exceed the Qualified Organization Base Period Amount (QOBPA). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(3), the QOBPA is defined as the sum of two distinct historical components: the Minimum Basic Research Amount (MBRA) and the Maintenance-of-Effort Amount (MEA):
QOBPA = MBRA + MEA

Both components rely on the taxpayer's historical "base period," which 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(B) defines as the three-taxable-year period ending with the taxable year immediately preceding the first taxable year of the taxpayer beginning after December 31, 1983 (representing the 1981–1983 period for calendar-year C corporations in existence during those years).

cells: Under § 41(e)(4)(A), the MBRA equals the greater of: (i) 1% of the average of the sum of amounts paid or incurred during the base period for (I) any in-house research expenses and (II) any contract research expenses, or (ii) the amounts treated as contract research expenses during the base period by reason of § 41(e) (as in effect during the base period). Under § 41(e)(4)(B), except in the case of a taxpayer that was in existence during a taxable year (other than a short taxable year) in the base period, the MBRA for any base period shall not be less than 50% of the basic research payments for the current determination year.

Ensures corporations exceed a baseline R&D commitment before accessing the 20% credit. Additionally, § 41(e)(4)(B) imposes the 50% current-year BRP floor specifically on taxpayers not in existence during a full taxable year in the 1981–1983 base period.

Under § 41(e)(5)(A), the MEA equals the excess (if any) of: (i) the average of the nondesignated university contributions (charitable donations to § 41(e)(6)(A) universities allowable under 26 U.S.C. § 170 and not taken into account for the research credit) paid during the base period, multiplied by the current calendar year's cost-of-living adjustment under § 41(e)(5)(C) (determined under § 1(f)(3)), over (ii) the amount of nondesignated university contributions paid by the taxpayer during the current taxable year.

Functions as an anti-recharacterization safeguard so corporations cannot manufacture basic research credits simply by reducing general philanthropic university donations under § 170 and relabeling those funds as § 41(e) basic research payments.

Any portion of current-year Basic Research Payments that does not exceed the QOBPA (BRP ≤ QOBPA) is treated as a standard contract research expense for purposes of 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), subject to the 65% limitation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A).
Preserves tax value for non-incremental payments by allowing 65% of the below-base amount to enter the general QRE pool for the regular or ASC research credit.

body.text: Federal Judicial Doctrine and IRS Audit Enforcement

The IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) Division has historically subjected research tax credit claims—particularly refund claims on amended returns supported by retroactive studies—to intensive examination, formerly designating research credit claims as a Tier I compliance issue. In the context of outsourced and university-sponsored research, audit disputes center on the "funded research" exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) (cross-referenced by Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(9)), alongside the contract research rules of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e). (Note that Treasury Regulation § 1.41-5 is currently marked "[Reserved]" for basic research for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986, leaving statutory interpretation to the text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(e), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e), and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d).)
The Substantial Rights Doctrine Under Lockheed Martin

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), a taxpayer cannot claim a research credit unless the research is performed on its behalf and it retains "substantial rights" in the results of the research. In university-sponsored research, academic institutions routinely mandate under institutional policy and the federal Bayh-Dole Act framework that legal title to any resulting patents vests in the university. The IRS has historically challenged corporate research credit claims where the sponsor or contractor did not obtain exclusive ownership of the resulting intellectual property.

The controlling judicial standard governing substantial rights was established by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000). In Lockheed Martin, the government argued that the taxpayer lacked substantial rights in its research because the federal government retained unlimited rights to use the technical data and disclose it to competing third parties, eliminating the taxpayer's monopoly advantage, and because federal export control laws restricted the taxpayer's functional ability to exploit the technology. The Federal Circuit rejected the IRS's position, holding that "substantial rights" must be determined by reference to the parties' research agreements and do not require exclusive rights. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and Lockheed Martin, so long as the agreement does not confer on another person the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research, and the taxpayer retains the right to use the research results in its trade or business without having to pay additional royalties or fees for that right, the taxpayer possesses substantial rights. For a corporate sponsor structuring a Section 41(e) agreement with a university, Lockheed Martin and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(3) dictate that even if the university retains legal title to resulting patents, the written agreement must explicitly grant the corporate sponsor at least a shared, non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free right to use the resulting research data and technology in its business without paying additional fees.
Financial Risk of Failure and the Performer-Sponsor Distinction
The second pillar of the funded research and contract research analysis concerns which party bears the financial risk of failure.

In Fairchild Industries, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Geosyntec Consultants, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), the taxpayers before the court were the engineering and defense contractors performing the research for clients, not the sponsors funding external researchers. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), the economic risk allocation rules operate symmetrically between the research performer and the research payor so that no more than one party to a contract may claim a research credit for the same expenditure.

When the taxpayer is the research performer (the contractor), under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), the performer can claim the research credit only if its right to payment is contingent on the technical success of the research, as in Fairchild Industries, where the U.S. Air Force was obligated to pay only if the contractor succeeded at each step and delivered acceptable prototypes. Conversely, if the client pays the performer on a time-and-materials, cost-reimbursement, or fixed-fee invoice basis where payment is not contingent on technical research success—as in Geosyntec Consultants and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, where the contracts merely required adherence to general professional standards of care—the research is "funded" by the client and the performer is barred from claiming the credit.

By contrast, when the taxpayer is the corporate sponsor paying an external researcher or university, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) mandates that an expense paid to an external party is eligible as a contract research expense on behalf of the corporate sponsor only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. As Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) explicitly states, if an expense is paid pursuant to an agreement under which payment is contingent on the success of the research, the expense is considered paid for the resulting product or result rather than the performance of research, and the payment is disqualified from being a contract research expense for the sponsor. Accordingly, for a corporate sponsor funding a university under Section 41(e) or Section 41(b)(3), the corporate sponsor must bear the non-refundable financial burden of the research expenditure even if the academic investigation fails to achieve its scientific objective. Simultaneously, to avoid disqualification under the funded research exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), the corporate sponsor itself must not be reimbursed for its university payments by an upstream third-party customer or government grant.
State-Level Basic Research Frameworks: California and Massachusetts

State legislatures leverage the structure of 26 U.S.C. § 41(e) to anchor corporate R&D expenditures and university endowments within their borders. California and Massachusetts exemplify how states modify federal basic research rules to advance regional industrial policy.
The California Paradigm Under R&TC Section 23609

California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 23609 incorporates the federal mechanics of IRC Section 41 by reference while introducing major statutory modifications that reshape corporate tax planning. Historically linked to the Internal Revenue Code as of January 1, 2015, California's general IRC conformity date was updated to January 1, 2025, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, following the enactment of Senate Bill 711 (the Conformity Act of 2025, signed October 1, 2025).

The most prominent feature of R&TC Section 23609 is California's credit rate structure. Under R&TC § 23609(a)(1) and (2) (modifying IRC § 41(a)(1) and (2)), while California's regular research credit for incremental in-house and standard contract QREs is 15%, California provides a premium 24% tax credit for incremental Basic Research Payments determined under IRC § 41(e)(1)(A). (For taxable years beginning in 2025 and later, SB 711 also replaced California's prior three-tiered Alternative Incremental Research Credit of 1.49%, 1.98%, and 2.48% with a 3% Alternative Simplified Credit—or 1.3% if the taxpayer had no QREs in any of the prior three years—while preserving the 15% regular rate and 24% basic research rate.) California's 24% basic research rate represents a 60% greater tax subsidy per incremental dollar invested than the 15% general QRE rate, and stands 4 percentage points higher than the 20% federal basic research rate, reflecting a deliberate state policy to channel corporate capital into California's higher education and scientific research institutions.

Beyond rate amplification, California statutorily expands the substantive scope of qualifying basic research. Whereas federal IRC § 41(e)(7)(A) restricts basic research to original investigations "not having a specific commercial objective," California R&TC § 23609(d) (and § 23609(h)(3)) explicitly modifies this definition to encompass "any basic or applied research including scientific inquiry or original investigation for the advancement of scientific or engineering knowledge or the improved effectiveness of commercial products," excluding only research related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Consequently, a corporate sponsor funding a California university to conduct applied scientific or engineering research aimed at improving the effectiveness of a proprietary commercial product qualifies for California's 24% basic research rate even though that identical payment would fail the federal "no specific commercial objective" mandate under IRC § 41(e)(7)(A).

To capture the economic multiplier of this subsidy domestically, R&TC § 23609(c)(1) and § 23609(d), as enforced through California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) Form 3523 instructions, impose an absolute geographic nexus requirement. Both "qualified research" and "basic research" include only research conducted physically within the State of California, meaning grants issued by a California corporation to an out-of-state university are entirely excluded from the California computation. Within California, R&TC § 23609 and FTB Form 3523 instructions also establish targeted biomedical and life sciences expansions of "Qualified Organizations" for basic research. Specifically, corporations engaged in qualifying biopharmaceutical research (satisfying designated 1987 Standard Industrial Classification Codes 2833–2836, 3826, 3829, or 3841–3845 and using organisms or cellular/molecular components to provide human or animal therapeutics or diagnostics) and biotechnology research and development (involving recombinant DNA technology or pharmaceutical delivery systems) are permitted to treat hospitals owned and operated by public universities (described in IRC § 170(b)(1)(A)(iii) and run by an IRC § 3304(f) institution of higher education) and "qualified cancer centers" (tax-exempt IRC § 501(c)(3) non-private-foundation entities designated as specialized laboratory cancer centers with Clinical Cancer Research Center status from the National Cancer Institute) as Qualified Organizations for the 24% basic research credit. Conversely, under R&TC § 23609(m) and (n) (redesignated § 23609(l) and (m)), California explicitly decouples from IRC § 41(b)(3)(D) and § 41(f)(6) relating to federal energy research consortia.

Despite these generous incentives—and the fact that unused R&TC § 23609 credits carry forward indefinitely—utilization of the California research credit is periodically constrained by California budget legislation and judicial precedent. During state fiscal shortfalls, the California Legislature enacted Assembly Bill 85 (2020) (codified at R&TC § 23036.3 and § 17039.3), imposing a temporary $5 million annual limitation on the application of business tax credits (including the R&TC § 23609 research credit) originally for taxable years 2020 through 2022, although Senate Bill 113 (2022) subsequently repealed the cap early for the 2022 taxable year. In June 2024, California enacted Senate Bill 167 and companion Senate Bill 175 (codified at R&TC § 23036.4 and § 17039.4), reinstating the $5 million annual limitation on business tax credit utilization for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027 (the 2024 through 2026 taxable years). For corporate groups filing a California combined report, the $5 million ceiling applies in the aggregate across all members of the combined reporting group rather than per individual corporate entity. Any credit disallowed by the $5 million cap has its carryover period extended by the number of taxable years the credit was not allowed (consistent with statutory suspension extension mechanics analyzed in FTB Legal Ruling 2011-04 for net operating loss suspensions), and under SB 175, taxpayers may make an irrevocable election to claim 20% of the capped credits per year as a refundable credit over a five-year period beginning in the third taxable year after the election is made.

Furthermore, California enforces strict entity-level credit siloing within unitary combined reports. Under General Motors Corp. v. Franchise Tax Board, 39 Cal. 4th 773 (2006), unlike federal consolidated return regulations where research credits offset the consolidated tax liability of the entire affiliated group, a R&TC § 23609 research credit can only be applied against the California tax liability of the specific unitary group member that generated the credit (absent a separate statutory credit assignment election on FTB Form 3523).
The Massachusetts Paradigm Under M.G.L. Chapter 63, Section 38M

Massachusetts governs its corporate research credit under Massachusetts General Laws (M.G.L.) Chapter 63, Section 38M, administered by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue (DOR) under promulgated regulation 830 CMR 63.38M.1 and Proposed Regulation 830 CMR 63.38M.2 (which governs calculation methods for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2015, as referenced in Massachusetts Schedule RC instructions). Under M.G.L. c. 63, § 38M, business corporations may claim a corporate excise tax credit equal to 10% of incremental Massachusetts qualified research expenses over a calculated Massachusetts base amount, plus 15% of Massachusetts basic research payments determined pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(1)(A).

Like California, Massachusetts enforces a strict geographic nexus under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(4) and (6) and Proposed 830 CMR 63.38M.2(2), (5), and (7), requiring that the underlying research activity take place physically at a "Research Facility Located in Massachusetts". Specifically, qualifying Massachusetts research expenditures are restricted to wages paid for qualified services performed physically in Massachusetts, supplies used or consumed in Massachusetts, computer rental fees for computers physically located in Massachusetts used for research taking place in Massachusetts, and contract or basic research payments attributable to research conducted at a research facility physically located in Massachusetts (with multi-state activities prorated by the ratio of days employed in research in Massachusetts). Under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(6), the Massachusetts Maintenance-of-Effort Amount (MEA) is similarly localized to nondesignated university contributions paid to educational organizations organized under the laws of Massachusetts. Unlike California's entity-level siloing, Massachusetts requires controlled groups and entities under common control (greater than 50% ownership) to compute the research credit on an aggregated group basis and allocate the credit among members based on their share of the group's total qualified research expenses and basic research payments.

In addition, Massachusetts coordinates its general corporate research credit with sector-specific incentives administered by the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center (MLSC) under M.G.L. Chapter 23I (alongside M.G.L. c. 63, § 38W). Certified life sciences companies conducting foundational biological, stem cell, regenerative medicine, biotechnology, or nanotechnology research aimed at relieving human suffering may receive MLSC authorization for specialized, refundable life sciences research tax credits that override standard M.G.L. c. 63, § 38M excise utilization limits (where standard credits carry forward indefinitely for portions disallowed by the $25,000 excise limitation and for 15 years for credits exceeding excise liability).

15% Regular Credit; 3% ASC (1.3% if no prior 3-year QREs) for tax years beginning in 2025 or later under SB 711 (replacing prior 1.49% / 1.98% / 2.48% AIRC).

body.text: IRC Section 174 Amortization, State Non-Conformity, and Section 280C(c)

Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) requires all creditable research expenditures to qualify under the federal R&E deduction and capitalization provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, legislative changes to Section 174 (and Section 174A) directly govern the tax accounting treatment of Basic Research Payments. Under the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, Congress eliminated the longstanding option to immediately deduct Section 174 R&E expenditures in the year paid or incurred, mandating instead that domestic specified research or experimental expenditures be capitalized and amortized ratably over a five-year period and foreign research expenditures over a fifteen-year period. Subsequently, on July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), which added 26 U.S.C. § 174A to restore immediate deductibility for domestic research or experimental expenditures for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (with transition elections for unamortized pre-2025 domestic balances), while retaining mandatory fifteen-year amortization for foreign research under 26 U.S.C. § 174.

This shifting federal landscape created a major federal-state compliance divergence in selective-conformity states such as California. Prior to October 2025, California conformed to the Internal Revenue Code as of January 1, 2015, and therefore never adopted the TCJA's post-2021 mandatory five-year amortization of domestic Section 174 expenditures. When California enacted Senate Bill 711 on October 1, 2025—advancing California's general IRC conformity date from January 1, 2015, to January 1, 2025, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025—the Legislature explicitly decoupled from the TCJA's Section 174 capitalization and amortization rules (and did not incorporate the post-January 1, 2025 federal enactment of Section 174A under Pub. L. 119-21). Consequently, throughout the post-2021 federal mandatory capitalization window and continuing under SB 711, California has continuously permitted corporate taxpayers to deduct 100% of both domestic and foreign R&E expenditures—including Basic Research Payments—in the current taxable year on their California corporate franchise tax returns.

Corporate taxpayers must simultaneously manage the anti-double-benefit rule of 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c). Under Section 280C(c)(1) (as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(b)(2)(B) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024), a taxpayer claiming the Section 41(a) research credit—which includes the Section 41(a)(2) basic research credit—must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in Section 174A(b)) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to capital account by the full amount of the research credit allowed under Section 41(a). Alternatively, under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(2) (formerly codified at § 280C(c)(3) prior to the TCJA redesignation), a corporate taxpayer may make an irrevocable election on a timely filed original return (including extensions)—via IRS Form 6765 for federal purposes and FTB Form 3523 for California purposes—to claim a reduced research credit rather than reducing its deductible or capitalizable research expenditures. Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(2)(B), the reduced federal credit equals the excess of the gross Section 41(a) credit over the product of that credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under 26 U.S.C. § 11(b). Because California's corporate tax rates and reduction factors (such as the 98.5% corporate-level and 87.7% shareholder-level credit reduction factors for S corporations under R&TC § 23609) and California's Section 174 deduction timing differ from federal law, corporate tax departments must maintain separate federal and state capitalization, deduction, and Section 280C(c) schedules.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Multijurisdictional Basic Research Credit Calculation

During the 2026 taxable year, Apex Genomics executes a contemporaneous written agreement with the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), a verified Qualified Organization under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(6)(A), to fund foundational algorithmic RNA sequencing research performed physically within California. While exploratory, the investigation is intended to advance scientific and engineering knowledge that may also improve the effectiveness of Apex Genomics' diagnostic software, satisfying California's expanded basic and applied research definition under R&TC § 23609(d) (and, assuming pre-competitive framing without a specific commercial product objective for the federal comparative row, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(A)).

Under the contract, Apex Genomics makes a qualifying cash Basic Research Payment (BRP) of $8,000,000 in 2026. Assume Apex Genomics has a historical base-period 1% R&D expense average of $1,500,000 under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(4)(A)(i) and a current-year Maintenance-of-Effort Amount (MEA) of $500,000 under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(5)(A) resulting from a reduction in its current-year nondesignated charitable contributions to qualified universities relative to its cost-of-living-adjusted base-period average.

Under the verbatim text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(4)(B), the statutory 50% MBRA floor states: "Except in the case of a taxpayer which was in existence during a taxable year (other than a short taxable year) in the base period, the minimum basic research amount for any base period shall not be less than 50 percent of the basic research payments for the taxable year for which a determination is being made under this subsection".

Under Scenario A (Legacy Corporation Exception / Unfloored MBRA), if Apex Genomics was in existence during a full taxable year in the 1981–1983 base period, it falls within the statutory exception of 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(4)(B) and computes its MBRA under § 41(e)(4)(A) at $1,500,000, yielding a total QOBPA of $2,000,000 ($1,500,000 MBRA plus $500,000 MEA) and an incremental creditable BRP of $6,000,000 ($8,000,000 minus $2,000,000). Under Scenario B (Statutory 50% MBRA Floor Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(4)(B)), if Apex Genomics was not in existence during a full taxable year in the 1981–1983 base period or is subject to the 50% floor under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(4)(B), its MBRA cannot be less than 50% of its $8,000,000 current-year Basic Research Payments, increasing the MBRA from $1,500,000 to $4,000,000, raising the total QOBPA to $4,500,000 ($4,000,000 MBRA plus $500,000 MEA), and yielding an incremental creditable BRP of $3,500,000 ($8,000,000 minus $4,500,000). body.text: Conclusion

26 U.S. Code Section 41(e) serves as a specialized fiscal mechanism within the Internal Revenue Code, offering eligible Subchapter C corporations a 20% federal tax credit on 100% of incremental cash payments made to qualified educational and scientific research organizations for foundational research above the Qualified Organization Base Period Amount. When paired with state R&D tax credit statutes—such as California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 23609, which elevates the basic research credit rate to 24%, expands substantive eligibility to applied commercial product research conducted physically within California, and permits immediate R&E deductibility despite federal capitalization rules, or Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 63, Section 38M, which provides a 15% basic research credit alongside refundable MLSC life sciences incentives—corporate-university partnerships can generate substantial multijurisdictional tax offsets.

Securing and defending these credits under IRS and state tax authority examinations requires strict adherence to statutory and judicial boundaries. Corporate sponsors must verify C-corporation eligibility under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(7)(E), execute contemporaneous written agreements prior to research performance with verified Qualified Organizations under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(2)(A) and § 41(e)(6)(A)–(D), retain non-exclusive royalty-free business use rights under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), ensure the corporate sponsor bears the non-refundable financial expenditure risk of unsuccessful research under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), accurately model the 50% MBRA statutory floor under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(4)(B) alongside the 65% QOBPA flow-through under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(1)(B), and reconcile federal Section 174 / Section 174A and Section 280C(c) elections with state conformity statutes (such as California SB 711) and unitary group credit limitations (such as General Motors Corp. v. Franchise Tax Board, 39 Cal. 4th 773 (2006)).
